headline: A gusty evening cold front ends Kentucky's mild spell before a likely freeze and chilly Tuesday; Upstate rain ends today, dense fog may form tonight, Monday turns warm, then cooler northeast flow returns Tuesday
disclaimer: Independent amateur analysis. This is not an official forecast or warning. Follow the National Weather Service and local authorities during hazardous weather.

refresh.workflow: Update and commit forecast.json once. GitHub Actions automatically locks the prior issue in forecast-history.json. Then verify the GitHub Pages URL; every Google Sites embed reads the same file and refreshes automatically.

kentucky.name: Central Kentucky
kentucky.subtitle: Danville primary · Lexington comparison
kentucky.summary: Mostly sunny, mild weather continues ahead of a northern-stream cold front today. The front crosses this evening and overnight with a band of rain, a gusty wind shift and modest rainfall. Strong cold advection and building high pressure then deliver a much cooler Monday, a likely freeze Monday night and a sunny but chilly Tuesday. Clouds increase Tuesday night as the next southern-stream system approaches, with rain possibly beginning near the Wednesday-morning 72-hour endpoint.
kentucky.currentConditions: At 8:00 AM EST, KDVK reported 37°F with a 32°F dew point, calm wind, clear sky and visibility above 10 miles. At 7:54 AM, KLEX reported 40°F with a 32°F dew point, southeast wind near 6 mph and clear sky. No official NWS point alert was active for Danville at the final issuance check.

days.label: Sunday / Sunday night
days.precipitation: 5% or less through afternoon; 85–95% evening and overnight
days.hazard: OFFICIAL NWS ALERT STATUS: no active point alert covers Danville at issuance. Independent concerns are wet roads, briefly reduced visibility and gusts around 20–30 mph with the evening and overnight cold front. Severe thunderstorms, flooding and advisory-level wind are not expected.
days.forecast: Mostly sunny and mild through the afternoon, with a most-likely Danville high near 69°F and southwest wind around 3–8 mph. Clouds increase late. A band of rain reaches the area mainly from about 8 PM–4 AM EST, plus or minus two hours, with 0.05–0.20 inch most likely and an isolated total near 0.25 inch. Wind shifts west and then northwest behind the front, with gusts around 20–30 mph. The most-likely Monday-morning low is near 43°F.

days.label: Monday / Monday night
days.precipitation: 10% or less very early; 5% or less afterward
days.hazard: No official NWS point alert covers Monday at issuance. The independent concern is a likely freeze Monday night, including a hard freeze in colder sheltered valleys. Daytime north wind will make the sharp temperature drop feel more pronounced; flooding and thunder are not expected.
days.forecast: Any leftover pre-dawn shower exits quickly. Clouds break as colder and drier air arrives on north wind around 7–12 mph with gusts around 18–25 mph. The most-likely high is near 53°F, followed by a clear, cold night. Applying the maintained Danville cold correction gives a most-likely Tuesday-morning low near 28°F, with middle 20s possible in the coldest valleys.

days.label: Tuesday / early Wednesday
days.precipitation: 5% or less through evening; 10–20% overnight, rising toward 30–50% after 7 AM Wednesday
days.hazard: No official NWS point alert covers Tuesday at issuance. Independent concerns are another freeze Tuesday night and a chilly northeast breeze. Most of the period is dry; rain associated with the next system may begin near the Wednesday-morning 72-hour endpoint.
days.forecast: Sunny and chilly beneath strong high pressure, with a most-likely high near 47°F. Northeast wind runs 5–10 mph with gusts around 15–25 mph. Clouds thicken Tuesday night as low pressure begins organizing to the south. The most-likely early-Wednesday low is near 30°F. The main rain remains beyond this period, although a few showers may reach Danville after about 7 AM Wednesday near the exact endpoint.

kentucky.bottomLine: Central Kentucky remains near 69°F today before an 8 PM–4 AM frontal rain band and a gusty wind shift. Most-likely Danville high/low pairs are 69/43°F, 53/28°F and 47/30°F. Monday and Tuesday are much colder, with a likely hard freeze in sheltered valleys Monday night. The main midweek rain remains beyond this forecast, although a few showers may arrive near the Wednesday-morning endpoint.
kentucky.confidence: High in today's temperature and tonight's frontal passage; high in Monday's cool-down and freeze; high in Tuesday's dry, chilly weather but moderate in the exact Wednesday-morning rain onset

upstate.name: Upstate South Carolina
upstate.subtitle: Clemson primary · Central/Pickens County comparison
upstate.summary: The weakening cold-air wedge keeps Clemson and Central cloudy with lingering light rain and very low ceilings this morning. Rain tapers by early afternoon, but residual moisture and light wind favor fog—possibly locally dense—late tonight into Monday morning. After fog dissipates, complete wedge erosion and pre-frontal warming support an unusually warm, dry Monday. A dry cold front passes Monday night, then high pressure north of the Carolinas rebuilds cool northeast flow Tuesday. Rain from the next southern-stream system may begin near the Wednesday-morning 72-hour endpoint.
upstate.currentConditions: From 7:50–7:54 AM EST, KCEU reported 57°F with a 56°F dew point, light rain, northeast wind near 6 mph and a 700-foot overcast; KLQK reported 56°F with rain, northeast wind near 3 mph and a 600-foot overcast; KGSP reported 54°F with northeast wind near 10 mph and a 500-foot overcast. No official NWS point alert was active for Clemson or Central. Tempest data was not used.

days.label: Sunday / Sunday night
days.precipitation: 40–50% through about 1–2 PM; 10% or less afterward
days.hazard: OFFICIAL NWS ALERT STATUS: no active point alert covers Clemson or Central at issuance. Independent concerns are wet roads and low ceilings this morning, followed by patchy to locally dense fog late tonight. Flooding, thunder, ice and hazardous wind are not expected.
days.forecast: Cloudy with light rain or drizzle lingering this morning and IFR to MVFR ceilings. Rain ends around midday or early afternoon, followed by gradual ceiling improvement and a most-likely corridor high near 64°F. Northeast wind runs 1–8 mph with early gusts around 12–21 mph, becoming light tonight. Areas of fog develop after roughly 9–10 PM; locally dense fog is possible toward Monday sunrise. The most-likely regional low is near 51°F, with station differences inside the calibrated range.

days.label: Monday / Monday night
days.hazard: No official NWS point alert covers Monday at issuance. The independent concern is morning fog, potentially locally dense. After fog dissipates, no meaningful hazardous-weather signal is present; the Monday-night cold front should pass mainly dry.
days.forecast: Areas of fog, potentially locally dense, persist through about 9 AM. Fog and low cloud then lift, followed by partly sunny, dry and unusually warm conditions as the old wedge fully erodes. The most-likely corridor high is near 72°F, with southwest wind around 1–7 mph and gusts below 15 mph. A mostly dry cold front crosses Monday night, turning the wind northeast and increasing clouds. The most-likely regional low is near 50°F.

days.label: Tuesday / early Wednesday
days.precipitation: 5% or less through most of Tuesday night; increasing toward 40–60% near or after 7 AM Wednesday
days.hazard: No official NWS point alert covers Tuesday at issuance. Independent concerns are a sharp temperature drop and breezy northeast wind. A widespread freeze is not expected, and the wind should limit fog. Rain may begin near the Wednesday-morning 72-hour endpoint.
days.forecast: Partly to mostly cloudy and considerably cooler behind the front, with a most-likely high near 58°F. East-northeast wind runs 7–12 mph, becoming 10–17 mph Tuesday night, with gusts around 20–26 mph. A classic pressure pattern rebuilds a shallow cold-air wedge. Most of the day and night remain dry, with a most-likely regional low near 38°F. Rain associated with the next southern-stream system may reach Clemson and Central around the Wednesday-morning endpoint.

upstate.bottomLine: Light rain and very low ceilings taper by early afternoon, followed by a locally dense fog risk tonight into Monday morning. Most-likely corridor high/low pairs are 64/51°F, 72/50°F and 58/38°F. Monday becomes dry and unusually warm; Tuesday turns sharply cooler and breezy as northeast flow rebuilds. Rain may begin near or just after 7 AM Wednesday. Tempest data remains excluded.
upstate.confidence: Moderate-high in today's rain ending and temperature; high in Monday's warm, dry afternoon but moderate in exact fog coverage; high in Tuesday's cooler northeast-flow regime and moderate in the exact Wednesday-morning rain onset

sourceNotes: OFFICIAL ALERTS: no active NWS point alert was present for Danville, Clemson or Central at the final issuance check. Official alerts remain separate from outlooks and this independent analysis.

The Louisville discussion and fresh point guidance support a mild, dry Sunday, a late-evening and overnight frontal rain band, 0.10–0.25 inch of rain, a sharp Monday cool-down, a Monday-night freeze and a dry, chilly Tuesday.

Chris Bailey's November 22 Kentucky Weather Center post, ‘Tracking A Big System for Thanksgiving Week,’ was accepted as authoritative published source material. Bailey calls for a windy and mild Sunday with 65–70°F temperatures, a gusty line of showers diminishing eastward tonight, much colder Monday and seasonably cold Tuesday. His larger Wednesday–Thanksgiving storm lies mostly beyond this candidate's valid period. Details absent from his post or unreadable in graphics were left unknown.

The Greenville-Spartanburg discussion supports lingering rain and low ceilings this morning, dense-fog potential Monday morning, a warm Monday, a dry Monday-night frontal passage and redevelopment of classic cold-air damming Tuesday night.

The Sunday Upstate high spread of roughly 60–66°F is resolved with a calibrated 62–66°F range and most-likely value near 64°F. Current IFR observations and the slower-clearing GFS support the cool side, while ECMWF and official guidance allow the middle 60s.

Official point guidance supports Danville near 69/43°F, 54/27°F and 48/30°F, and Clemson near 65/50°F, 73/49°F and 59/38°F. Independent calibrated ranges incorporate station corrections and model spread rather than copying the point values.

COD radar at 13:05Z and GOES-19 infrared imagery at 13:06Z showed Central Kentucky dry ahead of the western shower band while the Upstate remained beneath the Southeast precipitation and low-cloud shield.

Every currently available COD family was audited at 12:21Z: HRRR, RAP, RRFS, GEM-RDPS, GEM-GDPS, ECMWF, GFS, AIFS, AIGFS, CFSv2, GEFS, REFS, AIFS-ENS and AIGEFS. NAM, NAM Nest, SREF and continental HiResW ended operational production and were excluded as stale or unavailable.

Fresh locally installed BUFKIT 19 GFS, HRRR, RAP and RRFS profiles were consulted. Kentucky profiles place the frontal rain mainly between 8 PM and 4 AM with 0.05–0.20 inch most likely, while Upstate profiles support Tuesday's stable northeast flow, negligible CAPE and no winter precipitation. Older raw GRIB files were not allowed to override fresh guidance.

The WPC extended discussion supports a developing eastern U.S. storm beginning Wednesday. Because this candidate ends at 8:24 AM Wednesday, only the initial rain-onset risk is carried; the principal holiday-storm impacts remain beyond the valid period.
The maintained KDVK −1.5°F low correction and Kentucky empirical 5/5/6°F high and 8°F low widths were applied. Prose supplies one most-likely Danville value inside each calibrated range.
The maintained KCEU +1.5°F and KLQK −3.5°F low corrections preserve the Clemson–Central nighttime split inside current 10°F regional low ranges. Upstate high widths remain 4/5/6°F.
The latest completed accuracy summary contains 157 verified checkpoints across 55 forecasts and all-category accuracy of 81.4% overall, including 84.8% for Central Kentucky and 77.9% for the Upstate.
Current station corrections, empirical lead-specific widths, model records, calibrated confidence, explicit event windows, fog timing and official-alert separation were applied.
All local times use Eastern Standard Time. The third card includes Tuesday night and early Wednesday because validThrough is exactly 72 elapsed hours after issuance.
Contains modified ECMWF Open Data, selected and processed for independent forecast research under Creative Commons Attribution 4.0 International (CC BY 4.0).
Tempest data was not used for Upstate observations, verification, calibration or adjustment.
This is a candidate only. No repository, forecast history, website, widget or publishing workflow was modified during preparation.
